title: Running the notebooks
text:
Running the notebooksNotebooks 00–04 and the cheatsheet have their output already computed, so you can
read them without installing anything. These are saved examples: online controls do not
rerun the model. To change inputs and run exercises, open the notebooks locally in Pluto.
Notebook 05 is also available online in reading mode, with explanations, code and
exercises. To generate observations and fit the neural estimators, run it locally
with Julia and Python; follow the inference setup guide.RequirementsJulia 1.12 or later — install it with juliaup.
The committed Manifest.toml was resolved on 1.12.1; on an older Julia, delete it and
let Pkg.instantiate() re-resolve, which loses exact version pinning.Notebook 05 additionally pulls a Python environment (sbi) through PythonCall/CondaPkg
on first run — a few hundred megabytes. Notebooks 00–04 are pure Julia.SetupClone the repository, then run this once:git clone https://github.com/SGHoekstra/Behavioural_Macro_and_Finance.git
cd Behavioural_Macro_and_Finance/pluto_tutorial
julia setup.jl
That installs Pluto into your global Julia environment and every tutorial package into
the shared pluto_tutorial environment. Then launch Pluto:julia -t auto -e 'using Pluto; Pluto.run()'
Open any notebook from the Pluto file browser. Each notebook activates the shared
environment itself, so the same package versions are used throughout. The first
opening can still compile packages and functions; allow it to finish before changing
controls. Keep the terminal running while you use Pluto.OrderWork through 01 to 05 in sequence — each assumes the previous ones. 00 is an optional Julia
and Pluto primer, and cheatsheet.jl is a standalone reference to keep open in a second
tab. Exercises and interpretation checks are at the bottom of each notebook. Use fresh
variable names in your exercise cells; Pluto allows one defining cell per global
variable. Prefer Apply settings controls for expensive examples so changing several
inputs launches one new calculation rather than a sequence of reruns.Notebook 05 uses staged run controls and small demonstration budgets. Installing
its Python environment and increasing simulation or training budgets can take
considerably longer. Follow its guide before launching a full inference exercise.A useful workflowRead the question and predict a result before running the example.Record the calibration, seed, horizon and measurement units.Change one setting or mechanism at a time and compare like with like.Explain the result economically, including one assumption that limits the conclusion.Complete a core exercise before moving to the advanced extension.If a run appears slow, check Pluto’s running-cell indicator and the terminal before
launching another simulation. Start with the supplied defaults. Restarting Pluto is
useful after changing a model type or its methods, because those definitions can
persist within the Julia process.

title: Running inference exercises
text:
Running Notebook 05 inference exercisesRead the full notebook online.
It displays its explanations, code, exercises and saved figures from an actual
default run: the synthetic observation and the ABC, NPE and NRE-B results. The online
controls do not rerun the experiment. This guide explains
how to run its simulations and neural training in a local Julia/Python environment,
generate posterior draws and inspect how well the coefficients are recovered.Open the notebook sourceThe questionIn Notebook 04, you chose how strongly CANVAS firms pass demand, costs and expected
inflation into their prices. Can inflation and GDP growth reveal those three
coefficients instead?Notebook 05 uses a known-truth recovery experiment. It generates a synthetic
observation at chosen coefficients, then gives the estimator only the observation.
The true coefficients provide a reference for interpreting the inferred distribution.
All other model parameters and the pricing mechanism remain fixed.Before running, predict which pricing channel could be hardest to distinguish from
the others using just two aggregate series.Three ways to infer the coefficientsMethodWhat it doesWhat to inspectABCDraw coefficients from the prior, simulate data, retain draws close to the observationDistance definition, tolerance and accepted countNPETrain a conditional density of coefficients given simulated outputsNetwork fit, posterior shape and parameter correlationsNRE-BTrain a contrastive classifier to estimate a likelihood-to-evidence ratio, combine it with the prior and sample with MCMCNetwork fit, chain mixing and effective sample sizeThe executable example runs one prior-sampled round of each neural method. It uses
engines that can also run sequentially; calling an engine “SNPE” or “SNRE” does not
by itself add a second simulation round. The optional sequential exercise focuses
new simulations on the current posterior and explains why NPE needs a proposal
correction.A sharper histogram is not automatically a better posterior. Weak identification,
network error and a misspecified simulator can all affect the result.Run in stagesAfter cloning the course repository, follow the installation page and run:cd Behavioural_Macro_and_Finance/pluto_tutorial
julia setup.jl
julia -t auto -e 'using Pluto; Pluto.run()'
Open 05_likelihood_free_calibration.jl in Pluto. Opening the notebook starts in
reading mode: saved results and their plots are available, while new simulation
and training stages are disabled. Enabling the local
environment may install Python, PyTorch and sbi on first use.Enable the local environment. Read the observation protocol and small-budget settings.Generate the synthetic observation. Twelve quarterly inflation rates and twelve growth rates form a 24-value vector.Generate the ABC bank, optionally. Move its tolerance slider to reuse the stored distances without new ABM runs.Generate the neural training bank. Inspect the coefficient/output matrix dimensions and any failed simulations.Train NPE. Interpret all three marginals and inspect their joint relationships.Train NRE-B, optionally. It reuses the neural bank and samples using MCMC.The default experiment uses four simulated paths per output, 100 ABC parameter
draws and 200 neural training draws. NPE draws 1,000 approximate posterior
samples; the optional NRE run draws 200 MCMC samples. These are teaching budgets,
not an accuracy guarantee. Runtime varies by computer; start with the defaults
before increasing the cost.Match the observation to the simulatorThe synthetic observation and every training output use the same horizon, units,
four-path averaging and data transformations, with distinct seeds. Coefficient draws
use a separate random-number generator from the economy simulations.This averaged observation is an idealised experiment. An empirical application must
specify how data from one economy, measurement errors and transformations enter the
observation model. Changing the observation protocol requires changing training too.
Failed or non-finite simulations block neural fitting rather than being silently
removed from the estimation sample.Recovery, diagnostics and validationRecovery asks whether inference locates chosen coefficients in data from the same simulator.Inference calibration checks posterior probabilities across repeated held-out synthetic experiments.Posterior prediction asks whether posterior draws reproduce observed or additional features.Model and policy validation require independent data, alternative mechanisms or intervention responses.A same-model recovery exercise cannot establish that the model represents the real
economy or predicts a policy intervention reliably. Even good prediction of the two
fitted series can leave different pricing mechanisms observationally similar.Exercises to start withThe full notebook gives six exercises with hints. Begin with the two that need no
new economy simulations: vary the ABC tolerance and plot cost-push versus expectation
coefficients from the NPE draws. Then compare a coarser data representation, generate
a small posterior-predictive sample, discuss a misspecification test, or attempt a
second sequential round.For background, see Dyer et al. (2024),
Black-Box Bayesian Inference for Agent-Based Models,
and the official sbi Bayesian workflow
and sequential-inference guide.

title: Meet the model
text: A Pluto.jl notebook v0.20.24 frontmatter order 2 title "Meet the model" layout "layout.jlhtml" tags "tutorial" using Markdown using InteractiveUtils This Pluto notebook uses bind for interactivity. When running this notebook outside of Pluto, the following 'mock version' of bind gives bound variables a default value instead of an error . macro bind def, element format off return quote local iv try Base.loaded modules Base.PkgId Base.UUID "6e696c72 6542 2067 7265 42206c756150" , "AbstractPlutoDingetjes" .Bonds.initial value catch b missing end local el esc element global esc def Core.applicable Base.get, el ? Base.get el iv el el end format on end begin import Pkg Pkg.activate joinpath DIR , "..", "..", "pluto tutorial" io devnull import BeforeIT as Bit import Random using Plots, StatsPlots, PlutoUI, HypertextLiteral, DataFrames, Statistics, LinearAlgebra end md""" Notebook 01 — Meet the model Question this notebook answers what does the Austrian macro economy do over the next five years according to the Poledna et al. 2023 agent based model — and what is actually inside the box? We run the model first and look at its output, then open it up who the agents are, how they trade through the input–output network, what happens in a quarter, and whether the accounting closes. Lecture 2 slides covered Model overview slide "What are agent based model typical elements again?" Sequence of events in each quarter slide " i Expectations → … → v Accounting" How big is the model? agent count table Household behaviour and heterogeneity four types Firms Leontief production function , labour market search and matching Input output network , and the remaining sectors government, bank, central bank, rest of world Learning goals After this notebook you will be able to 1. Initialise, step and run the BeforeIT model, and plot any tracked series. 2. Name the agent types and read their counts off `model.prop`. 3. Visualise the production network and compare sector intensities. 4. Trace the per quarter event sequence by stepping manually. 5. Verify the GDP accounting identity — the stock flow consistency check. How to work through it first predict a direction of change, then run a short simulation, inspect the relevant quantities, and explain the mechanism. The online version has saved outputs use local Pluto to change inputs. Start with the default 20 quarter run and leave longer simulations until the end. A simulated path conditional on a 2010 calibration is not an assessment of forecasting accuracy. Forecast comparisons and Monte Carlo ensembles come in Notebook 02. """ md""" 1 — Load the Austria 2010 Q1 calibration The model ships with a fully pre calibrated parametrisation of the Austrian economy at the start of Q1 2010. The bundled parameters and initial conditions are calibrated using national accounts and additional statistical inputs. The calibration also involves behavioural specifications and estimated relationships loading the bundle does not remove modelling assumptions or establish its predictive accuracy. A few headline values from `Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1` VAT \tau^ VAT 15.29%, MPC \psi 90.97%, corporate tax \tau^ FIRM 7.70%. Read any of them off `model.prop` directly. """ begin nb1 p Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1.parameters nb1 ic Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1.initial conditions "Parameters and initial conditions loaded ✓" end md""" 2 — Initialise the model `Bit.Model` builds every agent and wires up the full stock flow consistent balance sheet structure. Note the scale. Lecture 2 quotes ~9.9 million agents for the actual Austrian economy, but `Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1` ships a 1 1000 scaled version — about 10,000 agents — so a run takes seconds rather than hours. Simulated agents represent larger populations. Aggregates and shares target the calibration, but integer rounding and a smaller economy can change finite population variation and network outcomes. These are synthetic agents, not individual administrative records. Part 2 below reports the simulated counts. """ nb1 model Bit.Model nb1 p, nb1 ic md""" Inspect what's inside the model. Each field is a container of agents or an aggregate tracker """ fieldnames typeof nb1 model md""" For example, the `bank` agent holds """ fieldnames typeof nb1 model.bank md""" 3 — Run the model Each call to `Bit.step ` advances the model by one quarter , running the full sequence from Lecture 2 | Step | What happens | | | | | i | Growth and inflation expectations are updated using fitted time series rules | | ii | Exogenous shocks drawn from 5 AR 1 processes | | iii | Credit and labour markets solved search and matching | | iv | Goods markets solved search and matching | | v | Accounting update balance sheets, check insolvencies, compute profits, taxes, transfers | We can step manually to see this """ begin model demo Bit.Model nb1 p, nb1 ic Bit.step model demo parallel true one quarter Bit.collect data model demo save the time series "Stepped one quarter. GDP round model demo.data.real gdp end , digits 2 " end md""" 4 — Simulate for T quarters `Bit.run ` is the convenient wrapper that calls `step ` `collect data ` in a loop. The default path runs when this notebook opens. Change the horizon and seed together, then press Apply simulation settings . Unconfirmed slider changes do not launch another simulation. Repeat simulation reruns the confirmed configuration a fixed seed should reproduce the same path in the same environment. Runtime depends on your machine and horizon. """ bind nb1 controls PlutoUI.confirm PlutoUI.combine do Child htl """ div p Horizon quarters Child "horizon", PlutoUI.Slider 4 4 40, default 20, show value true p p Random seed Child "seed", PlutoUI.Slider 1 100, default 42, show value true p div """ end label "Apply simulation settings", begin T horizon nb1 controls.horizon rng seed nb1 controls.seed nothing end bind run single PlutoUI.Button "▶ Repeat simulation" Markdown.parse "Confirmed horizon T horizon quarters T horizon ÷ 4 years . Random seed rng seed . The time series includes the initial observation at quarter 0." begin run single Random.seed rng seed m Bit.Model nb1 p, nb1 ic nb1 initial model deepcopy m preserve the same population before mutation Bit.run m, T horizon parallel false quarters T horizon, seed rng seed, initial gdp m.data.real gdp 1 , final gdp m.data.real gdp end end md""" 5 — Plot the results `Bit.plot data` knows how to plot any of the tracked time series. The 9 panel dashboard below shows the same quantities reported in Poledna et al. 2023 Table 4. """ begin ps Bit.plot data begin run single m end, quantities real gdp, real household consumption, real government consumption, real capitalformation, real exports, real imports, wages, euribor, gdp deflator, , plot ps..., layout 3, 3 , size 900, 700 end md""" Before changing the seed which quantities do you expect to be most variable? Then apply a second seed and compare. Both aggregate innovations and agent level random draws can change across seeds, and endogenous feedback can alter the path. A single seed cannot separate those sources of variation or identify an economic effect. Monte Carlo simulation quantifies variation under the specified model it does not capture every source of model uncertainty. """ md""" Part 2 — Anatomy of the model You have run it and seen the output. Now open the box who the agents are, how they are wired together, what happens inside a quarter, and whether the books balance. """ md""" 6 — Who are the agents? The Lecture 2 table "How big is the model?" reports ~9.9 million agents for Austria 2010 Q4 — the real economy. `Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1` is scaled 1 1000 so that a run finishes in seconds, so expect counts around a thousandth of the lecture's. Counts describe the scaled calibration small rounding differences are possible. """ begin p nb1 model.prop agent table DataFrame "Agent type" "Active persons including investor households ", "Inactive persons", "Domestic firms", "Government entities", "Foreign consumers", "Foreign firms imports sectors" , "Count" p.H act, p.H inact, p.I, p.J, p.L, p.G , agent table end md""" Total nb1 model.prop.H act nb1 model.prop.H inact nb1 model.prop.I nb1 model.prop.J nb1 model.prop.L nb1 model.prop.G agents — about 1 1000 of the lecture's 9.9 million, as expected from the scaling. One label needs care `prop.G` is the number of production sectors 62, the NACE breakdown , which doubles as the count of foreign supplier firms because imports arrive one representative firm per sector. It is the same `g` index used in `P bar g` and `firms.G i`. The four household types from Lecture 2 Employed `nb1 model.w act` — labour supplied to a specific sector. Unemployed — subset of `nb1 model.w act` with no current job. Investors — firm owners and the bank owner, receive dividends. Inactive `nb1 model.w inact` — outside the labour force, receive social transfers. """ md""" Let's inspect a single active worker """ fieldnames typeof nb1 model.w act md""" And a single firm """ fieldnames typeof nb1 model.firms md""" 7 — Household heterogeneity Lecture 2 identifies four household types . Regular workers are stored in worker arrays investor households are attached to firms and the bank | Type | Struct | Description | | | | | | Employed workers | `nb1 model.w act` `O h 0` | Earn wages, pay income tax, buy consumption goods | | Unemployed workers | `nb1 model.w act` `O h 0` | Receive unemployment benefits \theta^ UB w , job search | | Inactive persons | `nb1 model.w inact` | Out of labour force, receive social transfers | | Investor households | `nb1 model.firms` and `nb1 model.bank` | Own a firm or the bank, receive dividends \theta^ DIV 1 \tau^ FIRM \Pi i | Employed unemployed live in `w act` the `O h` field records which firm employs each worker 0 unemployed . There are `prop.I` firm owner households and one bank owner household. Their incomes and deposits are attached to the firm and bank objects. Therefore `length w act.O h prop.I 1 prop.H act` do not count firm owners twice or omit the bank owner when computing household shares. """ begin w act holds all regular workers employed unemployed O h 0 means unemployed O h regular nb1 model.w act.O h n employed reg sum O h regular . 0 n unemployed sum O h regular . 0 n investors nb1 model.prop.I 1 n inactive nb1 model.prop.H inact n total nb1 model.prop.H act n inactive het table DataFrame "Household type" "Employed workers", "Unemployed workers", "Investor households firms bank ", "Inactive persons" , "Count" n employed reg, n unemployed, n investors, n inactive , "Share of adults % " round. n employed reg, n unemployed, n investors, n inactive . n total . 100, digits 1 , het table end begin p wealth plot layout 2,3 , size 900,550 , left margin 4Plots.mm, bottom margin 4Plots.mm for row, snapshot, stage in enumerate nb1 initial model, "Initial population" , m, "After simulation" occupied snapshot.w act.O h . 0 groups snapshot.w act.D h occupied , "Employed", steelblue , snapshot.w act.D h . occupied , "Unemployed", crimson , snapshot.w inact.D h, "Inactive", mediumseagreen for column, deposits, group, colour in enumerate groups subplot id row 1 3 column if isempty deposits histogram p wealth, deposits subplot subplot id, bins 30, color colour, alpha 0.7, label "", title " stage group n length deposits ", xlabel "Deposits per simulated agent model units ", ylabel "Count", titlefontsize 8 else plot p wealth subplot subplot id, title " stage group empty " end end end p wealth end md""" Read the two rows as a comparison of the same simulated population. The top row is copied before the run the bottom row shows the population after the confirmed horizon. Membership can change through employment transitions, so these are group distributions rather than a panel comparison of fixed individuals. Initial deposits are assigned using the aggregate balance sheet calibration and model incomes. Equal assigned incomes can create narrow distributions within a group. Such distributions reflect initialisation assumptions, not observed microdata on household wealth. Simulation then changes deposits and employment status. Investor households are excluded from these three panels their deposits are attached to firms and the bank. Do not draw conclusions about their relative wealth from this figure. Income and wealth affect consumption budgets, but a heterogeneous deposit distribution does not itself imply heterogeneous marginal propensities to consume. Check your interpretation what would you need to compare these distributions with household survey or register data? Consider population weights, units, household definitions and the reference date. """ md""" 8 — The input–output production network Firms buy intermediate inputs from other sectors. The entry a sg describes input purchases from supplier sector s within buyer sector g 's intermediate input bundle. Columns are normalised over suppliers it is not the fraction of supplier s 's output sold to buyer g . This is the heatmap shown in Lecture 2 Figure "Intermediate consumption between 19 industries" . We plot the full matrix available in this calibration 62 sectors . """ begin nb1 a sg nb1 model.prop.a sg I O matrix rows supplier sector, cols buyer product heatmap nb1 a sg, color viridis, title "Input Output technology matrix a sg\n 62 NACE sectors × product types ", xlabel "Buyer product g", ylabel "Supplier sector s", aspect ratio equal, size 600, 550 , clims 0, quantile vec nb1 a sg nb1 a sg . 0 , 0.99 , cap colorscale at 99th pct end md""" Reading the heatmap a bright cell at row s , column g means supplier s has a large weight in buyer g 's input bundle. The diagonal entries represent within sector intermediate use e.g., agriculture buying agricultural products . Off diagonal bright cells reveal key supply chain dependencies — an upstream disruption can affect its customers. The size and persistence of that effect also depend on quantities, substitution restrictions, inventories, financing and market matching a bright cell alone does not establish a bankruptcy cascade. """ md""" 9 — Leontief coefficients by sector Recall the production function from Lecture 2 Y i,t \min\ \left Q^S i,t ,\ \beta i M i,t ,\ \bar\alpha i,t N i,t ,\ \kappa i K i,t 1 \right The three coefficients \bar\alpha i labour productivity , \beta i material efficiency , \kappa i capital productivity determine which input is the binding constraint in each sector. """ begin Each coefficient is a vector over firms take the mean per sector G sectors nb1 model.prop.G number of product sector types I s nb1 model.prop.I s vector of firm counts per sector Build sector indices sector id vcat fill s, I s s for s in 1 length I s ... leontief DataFrame "Sector" 1 length I s , "Firms" I s, "ᾱ labour prod. " mean nb1 model.firms.alpha bar i sector id . s for s in 1 length I s , "β material eff. " mean nb1 model.firms.beta i sector id . s for s in 1 length I s , "κ capital prod. " mean nb1 model.firms.kappa i sector id . s for s in 1 length I s , leontief end md""" 10 — Stepping through the quarter sequence Instead of running all T quarters at once with `Bit.run `, let's step manually and observe what changes. Each call to `Bit.step ` runs the full five stage sequence from Lecture 2 expectations → shocks → credit labour → goods → accounting . """ begin nb1 model step Bit.Model nb1 p, nb1 ic Snapshot before step gdp before nb1 model step.agg.Y e expected aggregate output emp before sum nb1 model step.firms.N i total employed workers rate before nb1 model step.cb.r bar policy rate Take one step Bit.step nb1 model step parallel true Bit.collect data nb1 model step gdp after nb1 model step.agg.Y e emp after sum nb1 model step.firms.N i rate after nb1 model step.cb.r bar DataFrame "Variable" "Expected output Y e", "Total employment ΣN i", "Policy rate r bar" , "Before" round gdp before, sigdigits 6 , round emp before, sigdigits 6 , round rate before, sigdigits 6 , "After Q1" round gdp after, sigdigits 6 , round emp after, sigdigits 6 , round rate after, sigdigits 6 , end md""" The small changes after one step reflect the exogenous AR 1 shock draw and the OLS expectation update. Multiple steps accumulate into the time series we plotted in Notebook 01. """ md""" 11 — SFC accounting check ✓ Stock flow consistency the central feature of the Lecture 2 model implies that the GDP expenditure identity must hold at every time step Y t C t I t G t X t M t BeforeIT computes GDP via the production approach internally, but also tracks each expenditure component. Let's verify they match. """ bind T sfc PlutoUI.confirm PlutoUI.Slider 4 4 40, default 20, show value true label "Apply accounting check horizon" bind run sfc PlutoUI.Button "▶ Run SFC check" begin run sfc Random.seed 1 m sfc Bit.Model nb1 p, nb1 ic Bit.run m sfc, T sfc C m sfc.data.real household consumption I inv m sfc.data.real capitalformation G m sfc.data.real government consumption X m sfc.data.real exports M m sfc.data.real imports Y prod m sfc.data.real gdp production side GDP Y exp C . I inv . G . X . M expenditure side GDP residual Y exp . Y prod max err maximum abs. residual rel err max err mean Y prod 100 DataFrame "Stat" "Max |residual| model units ", "Max relative error % " , "Value" round max err, sigdigits 4 , round rel err, sigdigits 4 , end begin run sfc plot 1 T sfc 1, Y prod, label "GDP production ", lw 2, color steelblue, xlabel "Quarter", ylabel "Real GDP model units ", title "Expenditure vs production GDP T sfc quarters ", plot 1 T sfc 1, Y exp, label "C I G X − M", lw 2, ls dash, color crimson plot 1 T sfc 1, residual . mean Y prod , label "Residual shifted to mean ", lw 1, color grey, alpha 0.6 end md""" The two GDP measures should overlay almost exactly residual near zero , confirming stock flow consistency in the simulated data. Note small floating point deviations 0.01\% are expected from rounding in search and matching they are not macroeconomically meaningful. """ md""" 11b — Check identities without cancelling errors BeforeIT exposes a `get accounting identities` utility that checks three simultaneous accounting identities. Let's run it and verify all pass. """ begin run sfc data sfc m sfc.data income residual data sfc.nominal gva . data sfc.compensation employees . data sfc.operating surplus . data sfc.taxes production nominal residual data sfc.nominal gdp . data sfc.nominal household consumption . data sfc.nominal government consumption . data sfc.nominal capitalformation . data sfc.nominal exports . data sfc.nominal imports real residual data sfc.real gdp . data sfc.real household consumption . data sfc.real government consumption . data sfc.real capitalformation . data sfc.real exports . data sfc.real imports cb bal, bank bal Bit.get accounting identity banks m sfc checked residuals maximum abs. income residual , maximum abs. nominal residual , maximum abs. real residual , abs cb bal , abs bank bal sfc table DataFrame "Identity" "Income production nominal GVA ", "GDP expenditure nominal ", "GDP expenditure real ", "Central bank balance sheet", "Bank balance sheet" , "Scope" "Maximum over recorded quarters", "Maximum over recorded quarters", "Maximum over recorded quarters", "Final model state", "Final model state" , "Absolute residual" round. checked residuals, sigdigits 4 , "Below 1e 3 model units" checked residuals . 1e 3, sfc table end md""" The first three rows use the maximum absolute residual across recorded quarters . Summing signed residuals could conceal offsetting errors. The bank checks concern the final model state, not every previous quarter. The tolerance is stated in model units for comparisons across calibrations, inspect residuals relative to the size of the relevant flows too. Passing these identities checks accounting consistency. It does not validate behavioural rules, forecasts or policy counterfactuals. """ md""" 12 — The firm size distribution Inspect the calibrated firm size distribution. A histogram helps describe heterogeneity, but does not test whether its tail follows a power law """ begin firm sizes nb1 model.firms.N i initial employment per firm histogram log10. firm sizes firm sizes . 0 . 1 , bins 50, title "Firm size distribution at t 0\n log₁₀ employees ", xlabel "log₁₀ employees 1 ", ylabel "Count", label "", color steelblue, alpha 0.7, end md""" A concentration of small firms and a few large firms is compatible with several distributions. A power law claim requires a tail threshold, an estimated exponent and comparisons with alternatives such as a lognormal. Here the figure describes the initial calibration it is not evidence that the model endogenously generates the empirical firm size distribution. """ md""" ✔ What you learned Running it `Bit.Model parameters, initial conditions ` builds the full agent population. `Bit.step model parallel true ` `Bit.collect data model ` advance one quarter `Bit.run model, T ` is the wrapper for T of them. `Bit.plot data model, quantities ... ` gives the built in dashboard, and `model.data.real gdp` reaches any tracked series. What is inside it About 10,000 agents across 6 types, stored struct of arrays. The real Austrian economy has ~9.9 million `Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1` is scaled 1 1000 so a run takes seconds. `model.prop.G` is 62 — the number of NACE sectors , which also fixes the count of foreign supplier firms, one per sector. The I O matrix `nb1 model.prop.a sg` encodes the production network — bright cells are supply chain dependencies. Leontief coefficients \bar\alpha i, \beta i, \kappa i vary across those 62 sectors. Stepping manually with `Bit.step ` lets you watch state change quarter by quarter. The GDP expenditure identity Y C I G X M holds to floating point precision — stock flow consistency confirmed. Exercises Exercise 01.1 — Sort the `leontief` table by \bar\alpha i labour productivity . Which sector has the highest labour productivity most output per worker ? Which sector has the lowest \bar\alpha i — i.e., is most labour intensive requires the most workers per unit of output ? Do capital productivity and labour productivity tend to move together across sectors? Exercise 01.2 — Compute the out degree of each sector in the I O matrix the number of sectors it supplies to `sum a sg . threshold, dims 2 ` . Plot as a bar chart. Which sector is the most interconnected supplier? Exercise 01.3 stretch — Form a hypothesis about which supplier disruption would be most damaging. Explain why out degree might be informative and why it could mislead. In Notebook 03, distinguish a model intervention from empirical evidence about a real sector. Starter code and checks Use new variable names in your exercise cells so Pluto does not see duplicate definitions. ```julia ex01 sorted sort leontief, "ᾱ labour prod. " rev true ex01 threshold 0.01 a 1% input bundle share, not a universal network definition ex01 links nb1 a sg . ex01 threshold ex01 outdegree vec sum ex01 links dims 2 ex01 indegree vec sum ex01 links dims 1 ``` Check 1 both degree vectors have one entry per sector. Summing all out degrees must equal summing all in degrees both count the same edges. Check 2 repeat at thresholds 0.001, 0.01 and 0.05. Does the most connected supplier change? State the threshold when reporting a ranking. Check 3 compare degree with weighted column shares, sector size and initial employment. Explain why a network count is not a welfare measure. Before Notebook 02 identify the initial observation at index 1 quarter 0 , the measurement units, and the difference between an accounting check and a forecast evaluation. """

Base.get el iv el el end format on end begin import Pkg Pkg.activate joinpath DIR , "..", "..", "pluto tutorial" io devnull import BeforeIT as Bit import Random using Plots, PlutoUI, DataFrames, Statistics, StatsBase end md""" Notebook 02 — Calibration, no burn in and forecasting Economic question how does a model start from an observed economy, and what evidence would make its forecasts credible? First inspect the calibration and balance sheets, then compare two initialisation experiments and two countries. Next build a Monte Carlo forecast and an AR 1 benchmark. Their final comparison shows forecast disagreement , not accuracy there are no held out outcomes in it. Lecture 2 slides covered Data based initialisation & no burn in , Data Sources and How big is the model? Calibration Process and The full parameter set almost no free parameters Out of sample forecast performance and Quarterly out of sample GDP forecast decomposition Learning goals 1. Distinguish data derived quantities, estimated coefficients and calibration choices. 2. Read initial sector balance sheets and recognise their units. 3. Test whether GDP remains near its initial level under different exogenous processes. 4. Compare country calibrations without attributing every difference to one parameter. 5. Build and interpret a fan chart, an AR 1 forecast and a horizon comparison table. How to work through this notebook Predict an effect before running an experiment, inspect the plot, and explain any surprise using the model's mechanisms. Defaults run when the notebook opens so the online version contains plots. For the expensive Monte Carlo section, change settings together and press Apply . Repeat buttons rerun the current settings they do not pause other reactive cells. """ begin nb2 p AT Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1.parameters nb2 ic AT Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1.initial conditions nb2 p IT Bit.ITALY2010Q1.parameters nb2 ic IT Bit.ITALY2010Q1.initial conditions "Calibrations loaded Austria and Italy ✓" end md""" 1 — Where do the parameters come from? The lecture groups the calibration into census business demography, input output tables, government statistics, regulatory or behavioural choices, and estimated time series blocks. The table below is a selection , not the complete dictionary. Some quantities live in `model.prop` firm characteristics and central bank coefficients live in their own objects. Counts are simulated agents , shares and tax rates are fractions, and the inflation target is a quarterly rate. Tax rates derived from accounts are effective rates rather than necessarily statutory rates. The consumption propensity `ψ` is a behavioural rule calibrated from income and consumption its label does not imply an independently identified causal marginal propensity. Before inspecting the values which quantities describe the initial economy, and which tell agents how to behave? Explore the full dictionary with `sort collect keys nb2 p AT `. """ begin nb03 m p Bit.Model nb2 p AT, nb2 ic AT p nb03 m p.prop param table DataFrame "Source block" "Census scaled counts", "Census scaled counts", "Census scaled counts", "Scaled counts", "I O tables", "I O sector accounts", "I O tables", "Government sector accounts", "Government sector accounts", "Government sector accounts", "Government sector accounts", "Government sector accounts", "Government sector accounts", "Regulatory calibration choice", "Regulatory calibration choice", "Benefit calibration", "Estimated export AR 1 ", "Estimated export AR 1 ", "Estimated government AR 1 ", "Policy target Taylor rule ", "Estimated Taylor rule ", "Estimated Taylor rule ", "Estimated Taylor rule ", , "Quantity" "H act", "H inact", "I firms ", "J government entities ", "a sg matrix dimensions ", "ᾱ i mean labour productivity ", "b HH g mean consumption share ", "τ^INC", "τ^VAT", "τ^FIRM", "τ^SIF", "ψ consumption propensity ", "θ^DIV payout share ", "ζ capital requirement ", "ζ LTV", "θ UB benefit replacement rate ", "α E export persistence ", "β E export intercept ", "σ G government innovation scale ", "π quarterly target ", "ρ rate smoothing ", "ξ^π inflation response ", "ξ^γ growth response ", , "Value" p.H act, p.H inact, p.I, p.J, " size p.a sg ", round mean nb03 m p.firms.alpha bar i , digits 4 , round mean p.b HH g , digits 4 , round p.tau INC, digits 4 , round p.tau VAT, digits 4 , round p.tau FIRM, digits 4 , round p.tau SIF, digits 4 , round p.psi, digits 4 , round p.theta DIV, digits 4 , round p.zeta, digits 4 , round p.zeta LTV, digits 4 , round p.theta UB, digits 4 , round nb2 p AT "alpha E" , digits 4 , round nb2 p AT "beta E" , digits 4 , round nb2 p AT "sigma G" , digits 4 , round nb03 m p.cb.pi star, digits 4 , round nb03 m p.cb.rho, digits 4 , round nb03 m p.cb.xi pi, digits 4 , round nb03 m p.cb.xi gamma, digits 4 , , param table end md""" Read the table critically. Data discipline many quantities, but the calibration also includes estimated exogenous processes, a policy rule and adopted behavioural regulatory choices. The last rows are examples of estimated blocks, not all estimated coefficients. Initialising from data does not by itself validate forecasts or policy experiments. The mean consumption share hides composition because shares sum to one inspect `p.b HH g` itself. An unweighted mean of firm productivity also hides its sectoral distribution. Matching an aggregate need not reproduce the heterogeneity relevant to an economic mechanism. """ md""" 2 — Initial balance sheets National and sector accounts supply aggregate stocks, which initialisation allocates across simulated agents. This is a data consistent construction, not an observed balance sheet for every individual household. The household sector includes active and inactive workers, firm owners and the bank owner counting active workers alone would omit some household deposits. Units matter deposits, loans and equity are stocks in the calibration's monetary units, whereas the policy rate is a fraction per quarter. Do not interpret a raw value as an individual amount in euros, or compare a rate with a monetary stock. """ begin model AT Bit.Model nb2 p AT, nb2 ic AT nb2 household deposits sum model AT.w act.D h sum model AT.w inact.D h sum model AT.firms.D h model AT.bank.D h bs table DataFrame "Quantity" "Household deposits all household types ", "Firm deposits sum ", "Firm debt sum ", "Bank equity", "Government debt", "Initial policy rate" , "Value" round nb2 household deposits, sigdigits 5 , round sum model AT.firms.D i , sigdigits 5 , round sum model AT.firms.L i , sigdigits 5 , round model AT.bank.E k, sigdigits 5 , round model AT.gov.L G, sigdigits 5 , round model AT.cb.r bar, digits 5 , "Unit" fill "Calibration monetary units", 5 "Fraction per quarter" , bs table end md""" 3 — Testing the no burn in idea A burn in discards an initial stretch of simulation because the starting state creates artificial transients. Data based initialisation aims to make the model useful from the reference quarter. The lecture's stronger diagnostic suppresses growth processes and asks whether the model fluctuates around its initial conditions. The experiment below is narrower it changes three correlated innovations while retaining the empirical histories used to form expectations. Compare two scenarios over 20 quarters five years 1. Baseline Austria 2010 Q1 with its normal stochastic processes. 2. Correlated innovations off `C 0` zero the covariance matrix for euro area GDP, export demand and import supply. Their deterministic AR 1 terms remain. Government consumption and euro area inflation still draw innovations using separate scalar `σ` values. A no growth comparison needs an expectations rule too. `Bit.STEADY STATE2010Q1` fixes exogenous processes and policy, and flattens the histories used by adaptive expectations. A constant history cannot identify an AR 1 slope and intercept separately the default refitting can fail numerically. That calibration is therefore not simulated in this exercise. An initial accounting balance alone does not establish a dynamically stable steady state. The horizontal line in the plot marks initial GDP, not a simulated steady state path. Predict, then inspect should removing these innovations reduce drift? Why is `C 0` not a complete no growth experiment? Compare the paths, but do not treat either as a full test of the lecture's no burn in claim or a proof that the calibrated economy is an exact fixed point. """ bind run noburn PlutoUI.CounterButton "↻ Repeat initialisation comparison 2 × 20 quarters " begin run noburn Random.seed 42 model shocks on Bit.Model nb2 p AT, nb2 ic AT Bit.run model shocks on, 20 C silences three correlated innovations, not all stochasticity. Random.seed 42 model no shocks Bit.Model nb2 p AT, nb2 ic AT model no shocks.prop.C . 0.0 Bit.run model no shocks, 20 "Two 20 quarter simulations complete. A fixed seed aids reproducibility each scenario has different dynamics." end begin gdp on model shocks on.data.real gdp gdp off model no shocks.data.real gdp Index each simulated scenario to its own initial value. nb2 index on 100 . gdp on . first gdp on nb2 index off 100 . gdp off . first gdp off nothing end begin p3 plot 0 20, nb2 index on, label "Baseline", lw 2, color steelblue, title "Initialisation comparison real GDP", xlabel "Quarters after initialisation", ylabel "Index own t 0 100 " plot p3, 0 20, nb2 index off, label "Correlated innovations off C 0 ", lw 2, color crimson, ls dash hline p3, 100 , label "Initial GDP reference ", color grey, ls dot p4 plot 0 20, nb2 index on . 100, label "Baseline", color steelblue, lw 2, title "GDP deviation from each scenario's initial value", xlabel "Quarters after initialisation", ylabel "Percent deviation" plot p4, 0 20, nb2 index off . 100, label "Correlated innovations off C 0 ", color crimson, lw 2, ls dash hline p4, 0 , color black, lw 1, label "" plot p3, p4, layout 2, 1 , size 750, 580 end begin dev on maximum abs. nb2 index on . 100 dev off maximum abs. nb2 index off . 100 Markdown.parse """ | Scenario | Maximum absolute GDP deviation from own t 0 20 quarters | | | | | Baseline | round dev on, digits 2 % | | Correlated innovations off `C 0` | round dev off, digits 2 % | The table measures the largest departure along each single path. It is neither a forecast error nor an across path standard deviation. In the `C 0` run, deterministic terms, the two remaining exogenous innovations and market matching can still move GDP. Interpretation task does the observed ordering agree with your prediction? Explain remaining movement before generalising. These paths illustrate initialisation under two stochastic specifications. Fixed seeds make the examples reproducible a difference between single paths does not measure an isolated causal effect. Neither establishes that every country or policy experiment starts at an exact fixed point. """ end md""" 4 — Austria vs Italy Compare the Austria and Italy 2010 Q1 calibrations. Counts refer to the scaled simulation, not literal national populations. Taxes, spending rules, industry structure, initial stocks and exogenous processes all change together. Prediction select one row and explain how it could affect demand or income. The country comparison shows joint differences identifying that row's effect would require changing it alone while holding the rest of the calibration fixed. """ begin pAT Bit.Model nb2 p AT, nb2 ic AT .prop pIT Bit.Model nb2 p IT, nb2 ic IT .prop comparison DataFrame "Parameter" "Consumption propensity ψ", "τ^INC", "τ^VAT", "τ^FIRM", "θ^UB unempl. benefit ", "θ^DIV dividend payout ", "ζ min. capital ratio ", "H act", "I firms " , "Austria" pAT.psi, pAT.tau INC, pAT.tau VAT, pAT.tau FIRM, pAT.theta UB, pAT.theta DIV, pAT.zeta, pAT.H act, pAT.I , "Italy" pIT.psi, pIT.tau INC, pIT.tau VAT, pIT.tau FIRM, pIT.theta UB, pIT.theta DIV, pIT.zeta, pIT.H act, pIT.I , comparison end bind run countries PlutoUI.CounterButton "↻ Repeat Austria–Italy comparison 20 quarters each " begin run countries Random.seed 42 m AT Bit.Model nb2 p AT, nb2 ic AT Bit.run m AT, 20 Random.seed 42 m IT Bit.Model nb2 p IT, nb2 ic IT Bit.run m IT, 20 gdp AT norm m AT.data.real gdp . first m AT.data.real gdp . 100 gdp IT norm m IT.data.real gdp . first m IT.data.real gdp . 100 inf AT m AT.data.nominal gdp . m AT.data.real gdp inf IT m IT.data.nominal gdp . m IT.data.real gdp p1 plot 0 20, gdp AT norm, label "Austria", lw 2, color steelblue, title "Real GDP", xlabel "Quarters after initialisation", ylabel "Index own t 0 100 " plot p1, 0 20, gdp IT norm, label "Italy", lw 2, color tomato p2 plot 0 20, inf AT, label "Austria", lw 2, color steelblue, title "GDP deflator", xlabel "Quarters after initialisation", ylabel "Price index t 0 1 " plot p2, 0 20, inf IT, label "Italy", lw 2, color tomato plot p1, p2, layout 1, 2 , size 800, 350 , legend topright end md""" Read both panels GDP is indexed to compare growth paths, not country size. The deflator is `nominal gdp real gdp`, a price level index, not an inflation rate . Quarter on quarter inflation would be `100 . diff deflator . deflator 1 end 1 `. Different paths do not establish that an MPC, tax or benefit parameter caused the whole difference. Even with the same seed, differing calibrations do not imply identical shocks. """ md""" Part 2 — Forecasting Data based initialisation gives the forecast an observed reference point without discarding an artificial spin up. It does not guarantee forecast accuracy. We now separate three questions where does the model predict GDP will go, how dispersed are its paths, and what held out data would be needed to decide whether it forecasts well? """ md""" Forecasting learning goals 1. Build a multi path Monte Carlo forecast and distinguish path quantiles from confidence intervals. 2. Estimate a simple AR 1 benchmark using only the pre forecast history. 3. Compare forecasts in the same units at horizons that were actually simulated. 4. Explain how conditional forecasting changes the available information. The lecture's forecast comparisons refer to the Poledna et al. study, published in 2023 earlier drafts appear in the slides . This short experiment teaches the workflow it does not reproduce the published forecast evaluation. """ md""" 5 — Monte Carlo fan chart A fan chart summarises simulated paths conditional on the same calibration and initial state . The published forecasting exercise uses hundreds of paths per reference quarter. Start here with 10 paths over eight quarters , then increase the budget only when you need a more stable estimate of the mean or quantiles. All paths start from Austria's 2010 Q1 calibration. One quarter is one model step, and array entry `h 1` is horizon `h` because the first entry is the initial state. We index each path to 100 at that point. The 10–90% and 25–75% bands describe model generated dispersion they are not confidence intervals for the ensemble mean or empirically verified coverage probabilities. Make a prediction will increasing the number of paths remove economic uncertainty, or only make its simulation estimate less noisy? Change settings below, then press Apply once. """ bind nb2 fc settings PlutoUI.confirm PlutoUI.combine do Child md""" Forecast settings Paths Child "paths", PlutoUI.Slider 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 , default 10, show value true Quarters ahead Child "horizon", PlutoUI.Slider 4 4 40, default 8, show value true Random seed Child "seed", PlutoUI.Slider 1 3000, default 2019, show value true, max steps 3000 """ end begin n mc fc nb2 fc settings.paths T fc nb2 fc settings.horizon seed fc nb2 fc settings.seed Markdown.parse "Applied budget n mc fc paths × T fc quarters seed seed fc . The initial state adds one observation to every path." end bind run fc PlutoUI.CounterButton "↻ Repeat forecast with the applied settings and seed" begin run fc Random.seed seed fc Serial execution makes this small teaching example reproducible independently of thread count. mc models Bit.ensemblerun Bit.Model nb2 p AT, nb2 ic AT for in 1 n mc fc , T fc parallel false, "Forecast complete n mc fc paths × T fc quarters." end begin Rows are horizons 0 T fc columns are Monte Carlo paths. nb2 gdp mat hcat m.data.real gdp for m in mc models ... nb2 gdp index mat 100 . nb2 gdp mat . nb2 gdp mat 1 1, nb2 gdp mean vec mean nb2 gdp index mat, dims 2 nb2 gdp p10 quantile nb2 gdp index mat t, , 0.10 for t in 1 T fc 1 nb2 gdp p25 quantile nb2 gdp index mat t, , 0.25 for t in 1 T fc 1 nb2 gdp p75 quantile nb2 gdp index mat t, , 0.75 for t in 1 T fc 1 nb2 gdp p90 quantile nb2 gdp index mat t, , 0.90 for t in 1 T fc 1 nothing end begin Draw bands by their endpoints a skewed distribution's mean need not lie inside every band. p fan plot 0 T fc, nb2 gdp p10, fillrange nb2 gdp p90, fillalpha 0.15, color steelblue, lw 0, label "10–90% of paths", title "ABM real GDP forecast n mc fc paths ", xlabel "Quarters ahead", ylabel "Index 2010 Q1 100 " plot p fan, 0 T fc, nb2 gdp p25, fillrange nb2 gdp p75, fillalpha 0.25, color steelblue, lw 0, label "25–75% of paths" plot p fan, 0 T fc, nb2 gdp mean, color steelblue, lw 2, label "Ensemble mean" end md""" Reading the fan the darker band contains the central half of simulated paths at each horizon the lighter band contains the central 80%. The mean is a separate line. Dispersion comes from the model's stochastic processes and matching, with parameters fixed. Longer horizons often have wider bands, but mean reversion, nonlinear dynamics and a small Monte Carlo sample can make widths non monotonic. More paths stabilise estimated quantiles they need not systematically narrow the underlying forecast distribution. """ md""" 6 — Historical trajectory and forecast overlay The history in `initial conditions "Y" ` follows the historical real GDP trajectory, rescaled to the model's output units during calibration. Its raw level is therefore not the same object as the model's value added measure `data.real gdp`. Index each series to 100 at its own 2010 Q1 value before overlaying them. The black line ends at the forecast origin. It supplies information available for fitting the benchmark it is not a held out future trajectory against which accuracy can be assessed. """ begin Y hist raw vec nb2 ic AT "Y" T hist length Y hist raw Y hist norm 100 . Y hist raw . last Y hist raw fc norm mean nb2 gdp mean fc norm p10 nb2 gdp p10 fc norm p90 nb2 gdp p90 x hist T hist 1 0 x fc 0 T fc p hist plot x hist, Y hist norm, lw 2, color black, label "Historical trajectory indexed ", title "History and forecast Austria 2010 Q1", xlabel "Quarters relative to 2010 Q1", ylabel "Index 2010 Q1 100 " plot p hist, x fc, fc norm p10, fillrange fc norm p90, fillalpha 0.15, color steelblue, lw 0, label "ABM 10–90% path band" plot p hist, x fc, fc norm mean, color steelblue, lw 2, label "ABM ensemble mean" vline p hist, 0 , lw 1.5, ls dash, color grey, label "Forecast origin" end md""" Check the join both history and forecast equal 100 at horizon zero. Indexing preserves relative movements but removes differences in level and units. It is useful for this teaching comparison it does not establish equality of the original accounting quantities. The fan reflects stochastic paths at a fixed parameter calibration, including random matching, rather than parameter uncertainty. A proper out of sample evaluation repeats the forecast at multiple reference quarters and compares predictions with subsequently observed GDP. The published application evaluates a sequence of reference quarters rather than this single origin. """ md""" 7 — A simple AR 1 benchmark Construct an intentionally simple benchmark using only the history up to the forecast origin `y t β α y t 1 ε t`. OLS chooses the intercept `β` and persistence `α`. Recursively applying `β α y` gives a point forecast no random innovation is added to it. Follow the code in three steps 1. Align `y lag` and `y now` so each row contains adjacent observations. 2. Add a column of ones for the intercept, then solve the least squares system with `X \\ y now`. 3. Start the recursive forecast at the last historical value, then index it to 100 for comparison. This is an AR 1 in levels , not an exact replication of the lecture's benchmark scripts, which use log differences for GDP and other variables. Transformations, estimation windows and data vintages matter when comparing forecast accuracy. A levels estimate near or above unit persistence can imply drifting or explosive long horizon paths inspect `α`. """ begin Y hist vec nb2 ic AT "Y" assert length Y hist 3 && all isfinite, Y hist "AR 1 needs a finite historical series." y lag Y hist 1 end 1 y now Y hist 2 end A row of X is 1, y t 1 coefficients are intercept, persistence . X hcat ones length y lag , y lag coef X \ y now β ar1, α ar1 coef ar1 forecast zeros T fc 1 ar1 forecast 1 last Y hist for t in 2 T fc 1 ar1 forecast t β ar1 α ar1 ar1 forecast t 1 end persistence round α ar1, digits 4 , intercept round β ar1, digits 4 end begin ar1 norm 100 . ar1 forecast . first ar1 forecast nothing end begin gdp norm nb2 gdp mean p10 norm nb2 gdp p10 p90 norm nb2 gdp p90 p benchmark plot 0 T fc, p10 norm, fillrange p90 norm, fillalpha 0.15, color steelblue, lw 0, label "ABM 10–90% path band", title "Forecast disagreement ABM and levels AR 1 ", xlabel "Quarters ahead", ylabel "Index 2010 Q1 100 " plot p benchmark, 0 T fc, gdp norm, color steelblue, lw 2, label "ABM ensemble mean" plot p benchmark, 0 T fc, ar1 norm, color tomato, lw 2, ls dash, label "AR 1 point forecast" end md""" 8 — Forecast divergence at selected horizons Compare the indexed AR 1 point forecast with the indexed ABM distribution. The table reports Absolute mean gap forecast disagreement in index points. ABM path standard deviation across path dispersion in the same units. Gap ABM standard deviation disagreement relative to model dispersion undefined when dispersion is zero. Within the 10–90% band whether the benchmark lies between those path quantiles. A gap of one standard deviation is a descriptive scale, not a significance test. Being inside the fan does not make the AR 1 accurate, and being outside does not make the ABM accurate. Neither forecast is compared with a realised outcome here. Only horizons within the applied simulation length are included. """ begin horizons filter h h T fc, 1, 2, 4, 8 nb2 mean gaps Float64 nb2 path spreads Float64 nb2 scaled gaps Union Missing, Float64 nb2 inside band Bool for h in horizons ar1 val ar1 norm h 1 abm val nb2 gdp mean h 1 gap abs ar1 val abm val spread std nb2 gdp index mat h 1, push nb2 mean gaps, gap push nb2 path spreads, spread push nb2 scaled gaps, spread 0 ? gap spread missing push nb2 inside band, nb2 gdp p10 h 1 ar1 val nb2 gdp p90 h 1 end nb2 divergence table DataFrame "Horizon quarters " horizons, "Absolute mean gap index points " round. nb2 mean gaps, digits 3 , "ABM path std index points " round. nb2 path spreads, digits 3 , "Gap ABM std" map x ismissing x ? missing round x, digits 2 , nb2 scaled gaps , "Within 10–90% path band" nb2 inside band, nb2 divergence table end md""" What would a proper forecast evaluation add? For each reference quarter, use only the information available then, simulate the required horizons, and compare point forecasts with held out observed values . For a fixed horizon, RMSE is `sqrt mean forecast . realised .^2 ` across forecast origins. Report its units and compare benchmarks using the same origins, horizons, information and transformations. Across path standard deviation is not RMSE, and the ABM mean is not observed truth. The lecture repository's `.. lecture 2 sfc abm tabs error table .jl` scripts show the larger evaluation workflow and require their own data. This notebook does not run that pipeline. Conditional forecasting fixes selected exogenous paths, for example external demand or government consumption, instead of drawing them. Realised future paths provide hindsight scenario paths supply assumed information. Such forecasts can reveal how external developments contribute to errors, but should be compared with benchmarks given the same information. """ md""" ✔ What you learned Data derived initial stocks, estimated coefficients and calibration choices have different roles. Aggregate household deposits include workers, inactive households and owners. Financial stocks and quarterly rates need separate unit labels. `C 0` removes three correlated innovations it leaves deterministic dynamics, two other exogenous innovations and random matching. A full no growth diagnostic also needs a well defined expectations rule an accounting reference is not a simulated steady state. GDP indices and deflator levels describe different objects inflation is a change in the deflator. Monte Carlo quantiles describe fixed calibration path dispersion, not uncertainty in the mean. A levels AR 1 is a teaching benchmark. Indexed forecast disagreement is not out of sample accuracy. Exercises — predict, implement, explain Work through 02.1–02.3 first. For simulations, construct a fresh model for every treatment `run ` mutates its argument, so running it again extends that path. Keep budgets small while debugging. Save an economic prediction before looking at the new plot. 02.1 — Compare like with like. Which rate or share differs most between Austria and Italy? Compare agent counts separately. Explain one mechanism linking your chosen parameter to demand or income, then state why the country comparison alone cannot identify its effect. Hint form `comparison.Italy . comparison.Austria`, but do not rank counts and fractions together. A consumption share vector contains more structural information than its mean. 02.2 — Covariance versus shock amplitude. In a fresh Austria model, apply `model.prop.C . 0.5` and compare its indexed GDP path with the baseline and `C 0` cases. Predict the change first. Which two exogenous innovations remain? Hint multiplying a covariance matrix by `f` multiplies standard deviations by `sqrt f `. To halve the correlated innovations' standard deviations, use `f 0.25`, not `0.5`. 02.3 — A small sensitivity experiment. Start with `f` in ` 0.0, 0.25, 1.0 `, a fresh model and the same seed for each run. Compute maximum absolute GDP deviation from each path's own initial value and plot it against `f`. Extend to ` 0.0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0 ` if useful. Is the relationship linear? Hint maximum deviation along one path is not a volatility estimator. Drift and nonlinear feedback can dominate it. Repeat a small set of seeds before claiming a monotonic relationship. 02.4 — More paths, the same economic uncertainty. Change the applied budget from 10 to 20 paths, keeping horizon and seed fixed. Compare the mean and 10–90% band. Try 200 paths only as an optional, more expensive precision check. Hint more paths reduce Monte Carlo error in estimated means and quantiles they do not remove model generated risk. A small change in band width can have either sign. 02.5 — Relative forecast dispersion. Compute the GDP coefficient of variation at horizons 1, 4 and 8 that fit within `T fc`. Does it increase monotonically? Hint for horizon `h`, use the row `nb2 gdp index mat h 1, `. Compute `std row mean row `, or multiply by 100 to report percent. Take the standard deviation across paths, not across time. 02.6 — An endpoint rather than a whole trajectory. Apply 20 paths and `T fc 20`, then compare the mean and standard deviation of GDP at horizon 20. Reuse the existing ensemble rather than running every model for another 20 quarters. Hint raw levels are in `nb2 gdp mat 21, ` indexed values are in `nb2 gdp index mat 21, `. State which units you report. Compare spread relative to the mean. 02.7 — Longer horizon diagnostic stretch . Compare fresh Austria and Italy models with `C 0` over 20 quarters, then extend a small set of seeds to 80 quarters. Which country departs more from its starting GDP, and does that ordering persist? Outline what else would need to change to construct the lecture's no growth diagnostic. Hint index each path to its own initial value, report the metric and horizon, and do not treat a single path as a stability proof. Removing all exogenous drifts and innovations is a stronger change than `C 0` flat histories also require an explicit expectations rule rather than an unidentified AR 1 fit. Future realised exogenous paths would instead change the information set of a conditional forecast. """
