text: A Pluto.jl notebook v0.20.24 frontmatter order 4 title "Shocks, expectations and policy" layout "layout.jlhtml" tags "tutorial" using Markdown using InteractiveUtils This Pluto notebook uses bind for interactivity. When running this notebook outside of Pluto, the following 'mock version' of bind gives bound variables a default value instead of an error . macro bind def, element format off return quote local iv try Base.loaded modules Base.PkgId Base.UUID "6e696c72 6542 2067 7265 42206c756150" , "AbstractPlutoDingetjes" .Bonds.initial value catch b missing end local el esc element global esc def Core.applicable Base.get, el ? Base.get el iv el el end format on end begin import Pkg Pkg.activate joinpath DIR , "..", "..", "pluto tutorial" io devnull import BeforeIT as Bit import Random using Plots, StatsPlots, PlutoUI, Statistics end md""" Notebook 03 — Shocks, expectations and policy Question how does a change to productivity or household spending propagate through a heterogeneous economy? Before running anything Predict which variable moves first, which balance sheets bear the cost, and whether the change is temporary or persistent. Then compare the prediction with the plots. The online page shows saved outputs use Pluto locally to change the controls. Lecture 2 slides covered What drives fluctuations? Five exogenous AR 1 processes Endogenous crises the bankruptcy cascade Expectations and fiscal monetary closure Learning goals 1. Distinguish external disturbances from endogenous propagation. 2. Design a matched shock baseline comparison and read its units and simulation uncertainty. 3. Test proportionality without mistaking Monte Carlo noise for non linearity. 4. Compare expectation rules and explain the euro area policy closure. """ begin nb3 p Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1.parameters nb3 ic Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1.initial conditions "Calibration loaded ✓" end md""" 1 — Five external processes, several propagation mechanisms The Poledna ABM models five external processes with AR 1 rules estimated from data. Their entry points differ the final GDP effect depends on the economy's response. | Process | Where it enters | First mechanism to investigate | | | | | | Export demand | `model.agg.epsilon E` | Foreign purchases of domestic output | | Import supply | `model.agg.epsilon I` | Availability of imported goods and inputs | | Government consumption | Government expenditure rule | Demand for goods | | Euro area GDP growth | `model.agg.epsilon Y EA` | The central bank's Taylor rule | | Euro area inflation | `rotw` inflation rule | The central bank's Taylor rule | The innovations for exports, imports and euro area output are drawn jointly using `model.prop.C`, a calibrated 3×3 covariance matrix. Government consumption and euro area inflation draw separately from their scalar standard deviations. Random goods market matching and innovations in learned forecasts add further simulation randomness. Read the dashboard carefully these are aggregate outcomes, not plots of the five innovations themselves. Co movement in one simulated path does not identify a causal effect. """ bind run baseline PlutoUI.Button "▶ Run baseline 20 quarters " begin run baseline m base Bit.Model nb3 p, nb3 ic Bit.run m base, 20 "Baseline run complete ✓" end begin run baseline plot Bit.plot data m base, quantities real gdp, real exports, real imports, real government consumption, euribor, wages ..., layout 2, 3 , size 850, 500 , title "Real GDP" "Exports" "Imports" "Gov. consumption" "Policy rate quarterly fraction " "Nominal wage bill" , end md""" 2 — Design a shock experiment BeforeIT calls `shock model ` every quarter after setting macro expectations and the policy rate, but before firms' pricing, production and household budgets. Our callable struct changes a parameter only when `model.agg.t 1`. Timing matters the productivity change and the consumption propensity change below remain in place after quarter 1. They are persistent parameter interventions, not one quarter pulses. The model continues to draw its usual stochastic disturbances. Change the controls and press Confirm together. The Run button repeats the confirmed experiment. Pluto also evaluates a modest default experiment when the notebook opens. """ begin nb3 shock controls bind shock settings PlutoUI.confirm PlutoUI.combine do Child md""" Shock type Child "kind", PlutoUI.Select "Productivity", "Consumption MPC " , default "Productivity" Multiplier 1.0 no change Child "multiplier", PlutoUI.Slider 0.80 0.01 1.20, default 0.95, show value true Monte Carlo paths Child "paths", PlutoUI.Slider 8, 16, 32 , default 8, show value true """ end shock type shock settings.kind shock size shock settings.multiplier n shock mc shock settings.paths nb3 shock controls end begin struct Nb3ProductivityShock mult Float64 end struct Nb3ConsumptionShock mult Float64 end function s Nb3ProductivityShock model model.agg.t 1 && model.firms.alpha bar i . s.mult end function s Nb3ConsumptionShock model model.agg.t 1 && model.prop.psi s.mult end Seed each replicate explicitly serial market matching avoids thread order noise. Resetting seeds aligns initial random draws. Endogenous branches can later consume different numbers of draws, so it does not guarantee identical future disturbances. function nb3 paths n shock Bit.NoShock , seed 4040, T 20 map 1 n do i Random.seed seed i Bit.run Bit.Model nb3 p, nb3 ic , T shock shock, parallel false end end end bind run shock PlutoUI.Button "▶ Run shocked vs baseline" begin run shock chosen shock shock type "Productivity" ? Nb3ProductivityShock shock size Nb3ConsumptionShock shock size models base nb3 paths n shock mc models shocked nb3 paths n shock mc shock chosen shock "Matched shock experiment complete ✓" end begin run shock nb3 dashboard map real gdp, "Real GDP", "Change % " , wages, "Nominal wage bill", "Change % " , euribor, "Quarterly policy rate", "Difference percentage points " , real household consumption, "Real household consumption", "Change % " , do field, panel title, units b hcat getfield m.data, field for m in models base ... s hcat getfield m.data, field for m in models shocked ... effects field euribor ? 100 . s . b 100 . s . b . 1 avg vec mean effects, dims 2 se vec std effects, dims 2 . sqrt n shock mc panel plot 0 20, avg ribbon se, fillalpha 0.2, lw 2, title panel title, xlabel "Quarter", ylabel units, label "Mean paired effect ± 1 MC SE", color steelblue hline panel, 0.0 label "No effect", color black, ls dash, lw 1 panel end plot nb3 dashboard... layout 2, 2 , size 900, 620 end md""" First check confirm a multiplier of 1.0 . All four differences should be zero, up to numerical tolerance. A GDP effect of −2 means GDP is 2% below its matched baseline a policy rate difference of 0.1 means 0.1 percentage points , not 10% higher rates. Next use 0.95. A lower productivity norm can tighten production capacity a lower `psi` reduces planned consumption relative to expected income. Trace the outcomes rather than assuming that both changes operate through the same mechanism. """ md""" Reading the four panels GDP and consumption show real quantity effects relative to their baselines. `data.wages` is the total nominal wage bill employment, wage rates and prices can all change it. The policy rate responds to euro area , not domestic, conditions. A domestic shock does not directly trigger an ECB rate cut in this model. Later rate differences can arise if the simulations' random draws diverge. The ribbon is one standard error of the mean paired simulation effect. It measures Monte Carlo precision, not parameter uncertainty or an empirical confidence interval. A persistent GDP loss alone does not prove a bankruptcy cascade. Inspect firm insolvency, bank equity or input shortages to distinguish mechanisms. Insolvent firms are refinanced in the baseline model they are not simply removed forever. Nonlinear DSGE models can also contain financial constraints, so this plot is not a general ABM versus DSGE verdict. """ md""" 3 — Is the response proportional to the intervention? Vary the productivity multiplier and compare real GDP at quarter 20 with one shared baseline ensemble. Each replicate uses the same seed across settings, and the no change case reuses the baseline itself. This supplies a useful zero effect check. The plot reports the mean of paired percentage changes, with a one Monte Carlo standard error ribbon. It is the terminal response, not the deepest recession within the horizon. A curved relationship is evidence to investigate, but a jagged small sample line is not by itself evidence of economic non linearity. Increase the number of paths before drawing that conclusion. The scan has seven settings to keep the default runtime manageable. """ bind run nonlinear PlutoUI.Button "▶ Scan seven productivity settings" begin run nonlinear shock mults 0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 1.0, 1.05, 1.10, 1.20 scan base nb3 paths n shock mc seed 4042 scan base mat hcat m.data.real gdp for m in scan base ... terminal effects Float64 terminal se Float64 for mult in shock mults scan shocked mult 1.0 ? scan base nb3 paths n shock mc shock Nb3ProductivityShock mult , seed 4042 shocked mat hcat m.data.real gdp for m in scan shocked ... effects 100 . shocked mat end, . scan base mat end, . 1 push terminal effects, mean effects push terminal se, std effects sqrt n shock mc end plot shock mults, terminal effects ribbon terminal se, fillalpha 0.2, xlabel "Productivity multiplier", ylabel "GDP change at quarter 20 % ", title "Proportionality check persistent productivity change", marker circle, lw 2, color steelblue, label "Mean paired effect ± 1 MC SE" hline 0.0 label "Baseline", color grey, ls dash vline 1.0 label "No change", color grey, ls dot end md""" Test a prediction under a locally linear response, a −10% intervention would give approximately twice the effect of −5%. Compare the 0.90 and 0.95 points and their ribbons. Do not call any departure a bankruptcy threshold without checking the underlying firm and bank outcomes. The graph combines all model mechanisms. """ md""" Part 2 — Expectations and policy Separate two mechanisms domestic expectations feed production and pricing decisions, while the policy rate is set from euro area conditions. The second mechanism does not provide direct feedback from Austrian inflation to the ECB in this calibration. """ md""" Question how do forecast rules and the monetary policy closure shape the simulated path? Learning goals 1. Read the learned AR 1 rule in the units used by the implementation. 2. Compare it with a last observation rule without calling either rational expectations. 3. Change one Taylor rule parameter at a time under the same initial seed. 4. Distinguish one illustrative trajectory from evidence across many simulations. """ md""" 4 — Learned AR 1 forecasts For a history `z`, `Bit.estimate next value z ` fits an AR 1 with an intercept and returns z^e t 1 \alpha t z t \beta t \varepsilon^e t 1 . The coefficients are re estimated by OLS each quarter. The implementation also draws a forecast innovation from the fitted residual variance this is a stochastic learned forecast , not just the conditional mean and not perfect foresight. `Bit.growth inflation expectations` applies the rule to log GDP and stored log price changes . It exponentiates the forecasts to obtain a GDP level and simple inflation rate expected growth is forecast GDP divided by the latest GDP, minus one. OLS fits the chosen forecasting rule to its history. It does not establish that the rule is optimal for the evolving economy or that expectations are rational. """ md""" 5 — Learned AR 1 versus last observation forecasts Learned AR 1 the default fitted rule, including its forecast innovation. Last observation expect no GDP growth and repeat the last observed inflation rate. Both use past observations. “Forward looking” versus “backward looking” would obscure that shared information set. The last observation rule also removes the default forecast innovation, so this comparison changes both the forecast rule and its noise. We specialise `Bit.growth inflation expectations` on a new model type rather than replacing a package wide function. That keeps the default rule intact for the other experiments. """ begin Bit. object mutable struct Nb3LastValueModel Bit.Model Bit.AbstractModel end function Bit.growth inflation expectations model Nb3LastValueModel idx model.prop.T prime model.agg.t 1 last output model.agg.Y idx last inflation expm1 model.agg.pi idx return last output, zero last output , last inflation end bind run expectations PlutoUI.Button "▶ Compare expectation rules 40 quarters " end begin run expectations Random.seed 1234 nb3 model ar1 Bit.Model nb3 p, nb3 ic Bit.run nb3 model ar1, 40 parallel false Random.seed 1234 nb3 const initial Bit.Model nb3 p, nb3 ic Wrap components that Bit.Model has ALREADY initialised. Reinitialising the tuple here would apply the shared balance sheet normalisation twice. nb3 model const Nb3LastValueModel nb3 const initial.w act, nb3 const initial.w inact, nb3 const initial.firms, nb3 const initial.bank, nb3 const initial.cb, nb3 const initial.gov, nb3 const initial.rotw, nb3 const initial.agg, nb3 const initial.prop, nb3 const initial.data Bit.run nb3 model const, 40 parallel false "Illustrative expectations comparison complete ✓" end begin run expectations p exp gdp plot 0 40, nb3 model ar1.data.real gdp, label "Learned AR 1 ", lw 2, color steelblue, title "Real GDP", xlabel "Quarter", plot p exp gdp, 0 40, nb3 model const.data.real gdp, label "Last observation", lw 2, color tomato, ls dash p exp defl plot 0 40, nb3 model ar1.data.nominal gdp . nb3 model ar1.data.real gdp, label "Learned AR 1 ", lw 2, color steelblue, title "GDP deflator", xlabel "Quarter", plot p exp defl, 0 40, nb3 model const.data.nominal gdp . nb3 model const.data.real gdp, label "Last observation", lw 2, color tomato, ls dash plot p exp gdp, p exp defl, layout 1, 2 , size 800, 350 end md""" What does this comparison establish? The two rules can generate different paths, but one path does not establish which forecasts better or creates more volatility. The same initial seed gives the same starting draws removing forecast innovations changes subsequent random number use, so later external disturbances need not match. For a stronger comparison, measure forecast errors and outcome dispersion across many seeds, and explicitly replay the same external disturbances. Distinguish uncertainty across simulations from fluctuations over time within one simulation. """ md""" 6 — The Taylor rule The implemented rule includes a real rate intercept and a zero lower bound \bar r t \max\ \left\ 0,\ \rho\bar r t 1 1 \rho \left r^ \pi^ \xi^\pi \pi^ EA t \pi^ \xi^\gamma\gamma^ EA t\right \right\ . It responds to euro area inflation and output growth, not Austrian conditions. Rates, growth and inflation are quarterly fractions in the code. Multiplying a rate by 100 displays its quarterly percentage it does not annualise it. The sliders start at this notebook's actual calibration values. Confirm a change to one coefficient, keeping the others fixed, then compare policy rates and domestic outcomes. """ begin nb3 taylor controls bind taylor settings PlutoUI.confirm PlutoUI.combine do Child md""" Smoothing ρ Child "rho", PlutoUI.Slider sort unique vcat collect 0.0 0.05 0.95 , 0.99, Float64 nb3 p "rho" default Float64 nb3 p "rho" , show value true Inflation weight ξπ Child "pi", PlutoUI.Slider sort unique vcat collect 0.0 0.1 3.0 , Float64 nb3 p "xi pi" default Float64 nb3 p "xi pi" , show value true Growth weight ξγ Child "gamma", PlutoUI.Slider sort unique vcat collect 0.0 0.1 3.0 , Float64 nb3 p "xi gamma" default Float64 nb3 p "xi gamma" , show value true """ end rho val taylor settings.rho xi pi val taylor settings.pi xi gamma val taylor settings.gamma nb3 taylor controls end bind run taylor PlutoUI.Button "▶ Run Taylor rule experiment 20 quarters " begin run taylor Random.seed 42 Default calibration nb3 m default Bit.Model nb3 p, nb3 ic Bit.run nb3 m default, 20 Custom Taylor rule via parameter modification nb3 params custom deepcopy nb3 p nb3 params custom "rho" rho val nb3 params custom "xi pi" xi pi val nb3 params custom "xi gamma" xi gamma val Random.seed 42 nb3 m custom Bit.Model nb3 params custom, nb3 ic Bit.run nb3 m custom, 20 "Taylor experiment complete ✓" end begin run taylor nb3 p1 plot 0 20, nb3 m default.data.euribor . 100, label "Calibrated rule", lw 2, color steelblue, title "Quarterly policy rate", xlabel "Quarter", ylabel "% per quarter", plot nb3 p1, 0 20, nb3 m custom.data.euribor . 100, label "Custom ρ rho val , ξᵖ xi pi val , ξᵞ xi gamma val ", lw 2, color tomato, ls dash nb3 p2 plot 0 20, nb3 m default.data.real gdp, label "Default", lw 2, color steelblue, title "Real GDP", xlabel "Quarter", plot nb3 p2, 0 20, nb3 m custom.data.real gdp, label "Custom", lw 2, color tomato, ls dash nb3 p3 plot 0 20, nb3 m default.data.nominal gdp . nb3 m default.data.real gdp, label "Default", lw 2, color steelblue, title "GDP deflator", xlabel "Quarter", plot nb3 p3, 0 20, nb3 m custom.data.nominal gdp . nb3 m custom.data.real gdp, label "Custom", lw 2, color tomato, ls dash plot nb3 p1, nb3 p2, nb3 p3, layout 1, 3 , size 900, 320 , legend bottomright end md""" Guided experiment first confirm the calibrated settings. The default and custom paths should coincide. Next change only ρ, then only ξπ, returning to the calibration between trials. Lower ρ reduces interest rate smoothing check the rate panel before interpreting GDP. Higher ξπ increases the response to euro area inflation, conditional on the lower bound. ξγ 0 removes the growth term it leaves the intercept, inflation response and smoothing. Record the quarterly rate difference in percentage points and the quarter 20 GDP difference in percent. One seed illustrates a mechanism repeat seeds before ranking policy rules. """ md""" Fiscal closure taxes, transfers, government purchases and interest payments enter the stock flow accounts. Accounting consistency tells us where a payment goes it does not by itself show that fiscal behaviour is empirically correct. These plots do not decompose taxes or government debt, so answering a fiscal question requires inspecting those series separately. """ md""" ✔ What you learned Persistent parameter changes differ from temporary shocks the model still draws other disturbances. A paired no change experiment should have zero effect. Seed each replicate and keep units explicit. Small ensembles can look nonlinear because of simulation noise a GDP path alone does not identify a cascade. The default AR 1 rule is learned and stochastic. Our alternative is scoped to a new model type. The Taylor rule reacts to euro area conditions, includes a real rate intercept and floors rates at zero. Exercises — predict, run, explain, check 03.1 — A diagnostic, not a result. Set the shock multiplier to 1.0 and confirm. Check all four panels. Why would independent unpaired simulations fail to give exact zero? Hint compare each baseline path with its own unchanged copy before averaging. 03.2 — Intervention timing. Compare productivity multipliers 0.95 and 0.90 at quarter 20. Is the larger effect twice the smaller one, within simulation precision? Check use the same seeds and increase paths before interpreting curvature. Explain why this is a persistent productivity change even though the hook mutates the parameter once. 03.3 — Policy closure. Set ξπ 0, leaving other coefficients calibrated. Before running, identify the external series the central bank now ignores. Check distinguish a GDP deflator level from an inflation rate and a quarterly rate from an annual rate. Do not infer a direct response to Austrian inflation. 03.4 — Two meanings of volatility. Run each expectation rule under at least eight seeds. Compute GDP's standard deviation across runs at quarter 20 , then compare it with the standard deviation over time within a run . They answer different questions. Hint `data.real gdp 21 ` is quarter 20 because index 1 is the initial observation. Report the seed count and avoid a universal ranking from one trajectory. 03.5 — Stretch a different monetary institution. Create a custom model type and specialise `Bit.central bank rate model YourModel `. Use domestic inflation in the rule, converting stored log inflation with `expm1`, and retain its intercept and zero lower bound. Check this changes the monetary closure it is no longer Austria taking the ECB rate as given. """

text: A Pluto.jl notebook v0.20.24 frontmatter order 5 title "Extending the model CANVAS" layout "layout.jlhtml" tags "tutorial" using Markdown using InteractiveUtils This Pluto notebook uses bind for interactivity. When running this notebook outside of Pluto, the following 'mock version' of bind gives bound variables a default value instead of an error . macro bind def, element format off return quote local iv try Base.loaded modules Base.PkgId Base.UUID "6e696c72 6542 2067 7265 42206c756150" , "AbstractPlutoDingetjes" .Bonds.initial value catch b missing end local el esc element global esc def Core.applicable Base.get, el ? Base.get el iv el el end format on end md""" Notebook 04 — Extending the model CANVAS advanced Question how does a persistent increase in firms' wage norms propagate, and how does the pricing rule affect its transmission? Before running anything Predict the first direct effect household income, firms' wage costs, or both? Then distinguish an inflation rate from a permanently higher price level . The online page shows saved outputs run Pluto locally to change the controls. Lecture 2 slides covered Pricing mechanism CANVAS Demand pull mechanisms CANVAS pricing mechanism implicit assumptions Sectoral inflation decomposition Learning goals 1. Add a model specific pricing method without replacing the base model's rule. 2. Read the local demand price signals used in CANVAS. 3. Compare shock effects against each model's own matched baseline. 4. Distinguish channel isolation experiments from an additive causal decomposition. """ begin import Pkg Pkg.activate joinpath DIR , "..", "..", "pluto tutorial" io devnull import BeforeIT as Bit import Random using Plots, PlutoUI, Statistics, StatsPlots nb4 p Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1.parameters nb4 ic Bit.AUSTRIA2010Q1.initial conditions end md""" 1 — BeforeIT's extension architecture BeforeIT uses Julia's multiple dispatch system to allow clean model extensions. The pattern is 1. Create a new model type inheriting from `Bit.AbstractModel`. 2. Define new method s for the function you want to override, specialised on your new type. 3. Julia automatically calls your method when the model is of your type. This is the "open closed principle" in action you extend behaviour without modifying the original source code. ```julia Step 1 new model type Bit. object mutable struct MyModel Bit.Model Bit.AbstractModel end Step 2 override a single function function Bit.firms expectations and decisions model MyModel your implementation here ... end Step 3 initialise fresh components with your type model MyModel w act, w inact, firms, bank, cb, gov, rotw, agg, prop, data Bit.run model, 1 calls your method, then records the quarter's outcomes ``` The tuple constructor performs the shared initialisation, including worker–firm assignment, balance sheets and the initial data point. For fresh components, calling the field constructor directly would skip those steps. `build canvas model` below uses the tuple constructor and then initialises CANVAS's planned supply field. """ md""" 2 — Read the CANVAS pricing equation P i t P i t 1 \underbrace 1 \phi^ DP \pi i^d t \text demand pull \underbrace 1 \phi^ CP \pi i^c t \text cost push \underbrace 1 \phi^ AE \pi^e t \text aggregate expectations . Each factor is a gross price multiplier. The channel signals are rates expressed as fractions a signal of 0.02 with a coefficient of 0.5 contributes a multiplier of 1.01. The product of the factors, not their sum, determines the price change. | Last demand versus planned supply | Firm price versus sector average | Adjustment | | | | | | Demand at least as high as supply | Below average | Price signal | | Demand at least as high as supply | At or above average | Output signal | | Demand below supply | At or above average | Price signal | | Demand below supply | Below average | Output signal | A coefficient of 1 applies the full computed channel signal it does not mean a 10% wage intervention becomes 10% inflation. A smaller coefficient attenuates that channel's direct effect. Its effect on persistence is a question for the model experiment, not a guaranteed consequence of the equation. """ md""" Information, timing and assumptions The firm compares its lagged realised demand with its planned supply and its own price with the sector average. Excess demand at a relatively low price signals scope to raise prices excess supply at a relatively high price signals a price cut. The other two quadrants adjust planned output. At equal demand and supply the adjustment signal is zero. This is a behavioural rule based on local information, not a derivation of optimal price setting. The experiment varies its coefficients by hand it does not estimate price stickiness or reproduce an empirical inflation decomposition. Check before coding changing a pricing method also affects production, profits, employment, expectations and later demand. Those feedbacks prevent a simple interpretation of each plotted line as an isolated direct price elasticity. """ md""" 3 — Implementing the CANVAS extension """ begin The CANVAS model lives in canvas model.jl so that this notebook and Notebook 05 share one definition instead of two copies that can drift. include joinpath DIR , "..", "..", "pluto tutorial", "canvas model.jl" "CANVASModel, its pricing override and build canvas model loaded ✓" end md""" 4 — Matched pass through experiments The intervention increases `firms.w bar i`, the firm specific wage norm , by 10% at quarter 1 and leaves it elevated. The model subsequently computes actual wages from this norm and production conditions actual wages and the aggregate wage bill need not rise by exactly 10%. Changing only `w i` at this hook would fail `set firms wages ` recomputes that field later in the same quarter. This is why understanding the step order matters when writing shocks. Compare each model's shocked path with its own unshocked baseline. Both model families use the same calibration and seeded replicate list changes to the pricing architecture can still alter later random number use. We run eight paths serially for a practical, reproducible default. Confirm the three coefficients together before rerunning. """ begin nb4 controls bind canvas settings PlutoUI.confirm PlutoUI.combine do Child md""" Demand pull ϕDP Child "dp", PlutoUI.Slider 0.0 0.1 1.0, default 1.0, show value true Cost push ϕCP Child "cp", PlutoUI.Slider 0.0 0.1 1.0, default 1.0, show value true Aggregate expectations ϕAE Child "ae", PlutoUI.Slider 0.0 0.1 1.0, default 1.0, show value true """ end phi dp canvas settings.dp phi cp canvas settings.cp phi ae canvas settings.ae nb4 controls end bind run canvas PlutoUI.Button "▶ Run CANVAS comparison 16 quarters " begin struct Nb4WageShock mult Float64 end function s Nb4WageShock model model.agg.t 1 && model.firms.w bar i . s.mult end function nb4 ensemble builder shock Bit.NoShock , seed 7, n 8, T 16 map 1 n do i Random.seed seed i Bit.run builder , T shock shock, parallel false end end ens field ens, field hcat getfield m.data, field for m in ens ... nb4 defl ens ens field ens, nominal gdp . ens field ens, real gdp nb4 infl d diff d, dims 1 . selectdim d, 1, 1 size d, 1 1 Exact price level gap. Its log is the cumulative difference in log inflation. nb4 price gap ens s, ens b 100 . nb4 defl ens s . nb4 defl ens b . 1 nb4 log gap ens s, ens b 100 . log. nb4 defl ens s . nb4 defl ens b The shared Ref is restored even if a simulation fails. function run isolated pair phi val shock Nb4WageShock 1.10 , seed 7, n 8, T 16 previous phi CANVAS PHI try CANVAS PHI phi val builder build canvas model nb4 p, nb4 ic ens b nb4 ensemble builder seed, n, T ens s nb4 ensemble builder shock, seed, n, T return ens b, ens s finally CANVAS PHI previous phi end end end begin run canvas wage shock Nb4WageShock 1.10 poledna builder Bit.Model nb4 p, nb4 ic ens poledna base nb4 ensemble poledna builder ens poledna shock nb4 ensemble poledna builder shock wage shock nb4 selected phi dp phi dp, cp phi cp, ae phi ae ens canvas base, ens canvas shock run isolated pair nb4 selected phi shock wage shock "Matched CANVAS comparison complete ✓" end begin run canvas p1 errorline 0 16, nb4 price gap ens poledna shock, ens poledna base errorstyle ribbon, errortype sem, label "Poledna baseline pricing", lw 2, color steelblue, title "GDP deflator after a 10% wage norm increase", xlabel "Quarter", ylabel "Price level above own baseline % " errorline p1, 0 16, nb4 price gap ens canvas shock, ens canvas base errorstyle ribbon, errortype sem, label "CANVAS ϕDP phi dp , ϕCP phi cp , ϕAE phi ae ", lw 2, color tomato, ls dash hline p1, 0.0 color black, lw 1, label "No effect" p2 errorline 0 16, 100 . ens field ens poledna shock, real gdp . ens field ens poledna base, real gdp . 1 errorstyle ribbon, errortype sem, label "Poledna", lw 2, color steelblue, title "Real GDP shock versus own baseline", xlabel "Quarter", ylabel "GDP change % " errorline p2, 0 16, 100 . ens field ens canvas shock, real gdp . ens field ens canvas base, real gdp . 1 errorstyle ribbon, errortype sem, label "CANVAS", lw 2, color tomato, ls dash hline p2, 0.0 color black, lw 1, label "No effect" plot p1, p2 layout 1, 2 , size 900, 410 , legend topright end md""" Read these units a price level gap of 2 means the GDP deflator is 2% above that model's baseline. It does not mean inflation remains 2 percentage points higher every quarter. A flat positive gap means the price level stays higher while the additional inflation has ended. Ribbons show one Monte Carlo standard error of the mean paired effect, not uncertainty about estimated parameters. 5 — Channel isolation experiments For a fixed reference with all three coefficients equal to 1, activate one channel at a time and compare its wage intervention with its own baseline. This reference is independent of the sliders above it always means all three coefficients equal to 1 . The decomposition uses 100 × log price level ratio , exactly the cumulative difference in log inflation. Isolated experiments generally do not add up to the full response. The plotted remainder collects the non additivity of all feedbacks it is not a uniquely identified structural contribution or only a second order cross product in the price equation. This experiment alone does not establish bias in an empirical regression. """ bind run decomp PlutoUI.Button "▶ Compare isolated channels and fixed full reference" begin run decomp ens b dp, ens s dp run isolated pair dp 1.0, cp 0.0, ae 0.0 ens b cp, ens s cp run isolated pair dp 0.0, cp 1.0, ae 0.0 ens b ae, ens s ae run isolated pair dp 0.0, cp 0.0, ae 1.0 ens b full, ens s full run isolated pair dp 1.0, cp 1.0, ae 1.0 ei dp iso nb4 log gap ens s dp, ens b dp ei cp iso nb4 log gap ens s cp, ens b cp ei ae iso nb4 log gap ens s ae, ens b ae ei full nb4 log gap ens s full, ens b full ei interact ei full . ei dp iso . ei cp iso . ei ae iso assert isapprox ei full, ei dp iso . ei cp iso . ei ae iso . ei interact qs 0 16 p decomp errorline qs, ei dp iso errortype sem, lw 2, color tomato, ls dash, label "Demand pull only" errorline p decomp, qs, ei cp iso errortype sem, lw 2, color steelblue, ls dash, label "Cost push only" errorline p decomp, qs, ei ae iso errortype sem, lw 2, color goldenrod, ls dash, label "Expectations only" errorline p decomp, qs, ei interact errortype sem, lw 1, color grey, ls dot, label "Non additivity remainder" errorline p decomp, qs, ei full errortype sem, lw 3, color black, label "All three coefficients 1" hline p decomp, 0.0 lw 1, color grey, label "No effect" plot p decomp title "Wage norm intervention channel isolation", xlabel "Quarter", ylabel "Cumulative log inflation difference 100 × log ratio ", legend topleft, size 850, 420 end md""" Interpretation checklist 1. All curves start at zero the intervention is applied after the initial observation. 2. Explain why raising wage norms changes both household income and firms' wage costs. 3. Compare a lower cost push coefficient with the full setting. Do not presume it lowers the total inflation response or increases persistence other channels can compensate. 4. The remainder is defined so the curves add up numerically. This identity checks the calculation, not the empirical validity of the channels. All coefficients here are chosen by hand. Notebook 05 introduces inference these runs are mechanism illustrations, not evidence about estimated Austrian or Dutch pass through. """ md""" ✔ What you learned Model type dispatch changes the pricing rule while retaining the base model's method. CANVAS combines demand relative price signals with cost push and aggregate expectations. A wage norm intervention must survive the model's wage update step. Each treatment needs its own baseline price level gaps and inflation rate differences use different units. Channel isolation experiments include economy wide feedbacks, so they are not additive direct effect estimates. This notebook changes pricing only the upstream CANVAS example also changes monetary policy learning. Exercises — predict, run, explain, check 04.1 — A no intervention check. Replace `Nb4WageShock 1.10 ` with `Nb4WageShock 1.0 ` in the main comparison. What should both panels show? Check use the same seed list. Restore 1.10 afterward. This changes the main experiment the fixed channel isolation experiment separately constructs its 1.10 intervention. 04.2 — Price level versus inflation. Run the default comparison. Find a quarter where the price level gap is approximately flat. Is the inflation rate difference also large? Hint compute simple inflation with `nb4 infl nb4 defl ensemble `, then compare each shocked path with its own baseline. Multiply rate differences by 100 for percentage points. 04.3 — Turn off direct cost push. Set ϕCP 0, keep the other coefficients at 1, and confirm. Predict whether higher household income can still alter demand and prices. Check compare the full reference with the cost push only curve. Zeroing one pricing channel does not switch off wage payments or the other channels. 04.4 — Persistence without assuming it. Compare ϕAE 1 and ϕAE 0 with the same other settings. Record the quarter 16 price level gap and the quarterly inflation differences. Hint a higher terminal price level and persistent extra inflation are different claims. Repeat the seed list before drawing a general conclusion about expectation feedback. 04.5 — Interpret the remainder. Verify that the isolated curves plus the remainder recover the full reference curve. Explain why this arithmetic identity does not identify an empirical interaction coefficient or prove that a single equation estimate is biased. """
